title: Why Arab armies don't win wars - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Reviewing Kenneth Pollack's Armies of Sand, the piece argues that the repeated battlefield underperformance of Arab militaries — despite advantages in men and materiel — is not explained by Soviet doctrine or politicization, but by deep cultural patterns (deference to authority, in-group loyalty, honor/shame) transmitted through rote-memorization education and reproduced in civilian bureaucracies. The same traits that produced the 1967 collapse and Saddam's failed Iran offensive are held to obstruct present-day social and economic reform across the region.

themes.theme: Materiel advantage does not predict outcomes

insights.claim: Arab militaries have repeatedly lost wars while enjoying numerical advantages in troops, tanks and aircraft, meaning order-of-battle counts are a poor predictor of regional military outcomes.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: When pricing escalation risk in the Middle East, weight force-employment quality over headline hardware inventories; conventional Arab-state coalitions have historically under-delivered relative to their paper strength.
insights.quote: the coalition of Arab states lose 70,000 square kilometers of territory, despite fielding many more troops, tanks, and aircraft than their Israeli opponents
insights.locator: Nasser’s commanders hadn’t been entirely honest

insights.claim: In the opening hours of the Six-Day War on 5 June 1967, Israel destroyed 298 of Egypt's 420 combat aircraft on the tarmac, and the Arab coalition ultimately lost 70,000 square kilometers of territory.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A concrete base rate for how fast a regional air campaign can decide a conflict — relevant to how quickly oil and shipping risk premia can be priced in or out.
insights.locator: In the early hours of 5th June 1967

insights.claim: The pattern of underperformance is not specific to fighting Israel: Gaddafi's Libya lost repeatedly to poverty-stricken Chad, and Saddam Hussein's offensive against Iran is characterized as one of the most pathetic military offensives of the past century.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Rules out 'Israeli exceptionalism' as the explanation, so the weakness should be assumed to persist in any conventional conflict these states enter, not just Arab-Israeli ones.
insights.quote: one of the most pathetic military offensives of the past century
insights.locator: In Armies of Sand, former CIA analyst Kenneth Pollack

insights.claim: The Soviet-doctrine explanation for Arab military failure is rebutted by the fact that Cuba and North Korea also relied on Soviet doctrine and performed creditably in their twentieth-century engagements.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Analysts using 'they trained Soviet-style' as shorthand for military weakness are applying a variable that does not travel; discount that heuristic when assessing any client military.

insights.claim: Politicization of the officer corps also fails as an explanation because Egyptian military performance remained as dismal as ever after substantial depoliticization in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Implies institutional reform of a defense ministry alone will not raise combat effectiveness — so defense spending and restructuring headlines should not be read as capability gains.

insights.claim: Coup-proofing produces extreme institutional duplication: Saddam Hussein at one point ran as many as sixteen separate security services that spent an inordinate amount of time spying on each other.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A benchmark for how regimes that fear their own militaries allocate resources — fragmented security architecture signals internal regime fragility more than external capability.

insights.claim: Pollack's core framework attributes battlefield failure to cultural patterns — deference to authority, in-group loyalty over outsiders, a premium on personal honor and horror of shame — with shame explaining falsified reporting up the chain and deference explaining officers obeying obsolete orders.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A reusable model for judging whether any hierarchical organization will surface bad news in time — applicable to state-owned enterprises and sovereign data as well as armies.
insights.quote: The fear of shame explains why Nasser’s commanders told him he was winning, while the deference to hierarchy explains why battalion officers would stick to orders long after they ceased to make sense.
insights.locator: Instead, he argues that these failures stem from patterns

insights.claim: The transmission mechanism is pedagogy: mass public school systems built in the 1950s and 60s changed the syllabus but preserved the Quranic-school teaching methods that emphasize rote learning over problem solving, and that habit carries into military training built on rehearsing pre-scripted maneuvers.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Implies improvement is generational and curriculum-deep, not procurement-deep — a long lead time before human-capital reforms show up in either military or productivity data.
insights.quote: they changed the syllabus but preserved the teaching methods, which emphasize rote learning over problem solving
insights.locator: When governments built mass public school systems

insights.claim: Scripted training extends to elite units: an American trainer of Egypt's F-16 pilots reported that before exercises began they knew where to turn, where to pretend to fire, and who would win, and became extremely upset when anyone deviated.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Advanced Western platforms sold into the region may not translate into effectiveness; arms-export headlines overstate the capability shift they create.
insights.quote: they know where to turn, and where to pretend to fire munitions, and who is going to win
insights.locator: This tendency seeps into military training

insights.claim: The Yom Kippur War offers a concrete case of doctrine-over-initiative failure: after breaking through Israeli defenses on the Golan Heights in 1973, Syrian troops paused in line with their pre-war plan, letting Israel rush reserves forward and retake the territory.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Breakthroughs by these forces should not be extrapolated into decisive outcomes — initial territorial gains have historically been reversible within days.
insights.locator: During the Yom Kippur War of 1973

themes.theme: Exceptions, bureaucracy and the reform read-across

insights.claim: The capable exceptions are selection effects rather than counterexamples: Hezbollah became highly effective only after shrinking its ranks post-Lebanese Civil War to retain a small minority of culturally atypical proven fighters, and Islamic State at its 2014 peak drew its most gifted commanders from Chechens, Uzbeks and Tajiks.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Small, self-selected non-state forces can outfight far larger state armies in the region — asymmetric actors deserve more weight in escalation scenarios than state order-of-battle suggests.
insights.locator: The exceptions largely support Pollack’s case

insights.claim: The same authority-concentrating, risk-averse pattern is documented in civilian institutions: in one study of Egyptian, Saudi and Sudanese bureaucracies, 90 percent of senior officials deemed their subordinates unqualified to innovate.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A hard number on delegation failure in regional bureaucracies — a drag on execution risk for state-led megaprojects and diversification plans that depend on middle-management initiative.
insights.quote: 90 percent of senior officials deemed their subordinates ‘unqualified to innovate’
insights.locator: In most Arab offices and government ministries

insights.claim: The author's closing implied view is that these organizational traits are visible in everyday Middle Eastern banks and government ministries and continue to obstruct the region's social and economic reform efforts, not just its militaries.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Treat announced regional reform and diversification programs with implementation skepticism; the binding constraint is described as cultural-institutional, which moves on decade timescales.
insights.quote: They continue to pose a challenge for regional efforts at social and economic reform.
insights.locator: Anyone who has interacted with a bank or government ministry
